opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to put it is that in a standard transformer, inference is purely a read operation. You train the model, the weights get frozen, and at test time all the "learning" the model can do is in-context: it's attending over the tokens in its window. Once that context is gone, nothing persists. The parameters never change from the interaction itself.

In Hope, inference and learning are not really separate phases. That comes from the nested learning perspective: we think of the model as a set of nested optimization problems, each with its own context flow and its own update frequency. So when Hope processes a sequence at test time, some of its components are actually being updated. They're learning to compress and memorize the incoming context, rather than just attending over it.

There are two pieces that make this work. First, the self-modifying part. Hope builds on the Titans line of work, where you have a neural long-term memory that's updated by a learning rule based on how "surprising" the incoming tokens are. In Hope, the model goes a step further and learns its own update rule, so it's modifying how it modifies itself, in a sense.

Second, and I think this is the more important conceptual shift, is what we call the continuum memory system. In a transformer you basically have two extremes: attention, which is very short-term and updates every token, and the MLP weights, which are long-term and effectively update never after pretraining. We think that dichotomy is kind of artificial. So in Hope you have a spectrum of memory blocks that update at different frequencies. Some update quickly and capture very local information. Others update more slowly and consolidate knowledge over longer horizons. It's loosely inspired by how the brain has different timescales of consolidation.

So practically, what that means at inference is that the model isn't limited to "what's in my window right now" versus "what I learned in pretraining." There's this whole middle ground where it can keep adapting as it sees more data. That's important for things like continual learning and very long context, where with a transformer you either pay quadratic cost or you just lose information.

Of course, it comes with its own challenges. You're doing optimization inside the forward pass, so you have to think carefully about efficiency, about parallelizing those inner updates, and about stability. But conceptually, the big difference is that a transformer at inference is a fixed function, while Hope at inference is still a learning system.

r002.rationale: It describes compressing incoming context, but does not state that a scheduled MLP weight update uses all tokens seen so far in the current chunk.

r003.rationale: It says some components update during inference, but does not specify that a due MLP block updates its weights before performing inference.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to put it is that in a standard transformer, inference is fundamentally a frozen process. You train the model, you fix the weights, and then at test time all the "learning," if you want to call it that, happens inside the context window. The attention mechanism is essentially a lookup over the key-value cache. It's very powerful, but nothing about the model itself is changing while it reads your input. The parameters at token one are identical to the parameters at token one million.

With Hope, and really with the whole nested learning view that it comes out of, we're trying to blur that line between training and inference. The idea is that inference should itself be a learning process. So as the model processes a sequence, there are components, we call them continuum memory, that are actually updating their own parameters online, with their own objectives, at different frequencies. Some pieces update every token, some update every few hundred tokens, some are essentially static like the transformer's weights. You get this spectrum rather than a binary between "frozen weights" and "context."

And the reason that matters is that it changes what memory means. In a transformer, long-term memory is the pretrained weights, and short-term memory is the context, and there's nothing in between. If something falls out of the context window, it's gone. In Hope, information from the sequence gets compressed into the fast-updating parameters, so the model is genuinely consolidating what it sees, a little bit like how you'd think about memory consolidation in the brain. You're not just retrieving, you're adapting.

The other piece I'd emphasize is the self-referential aspect. We designed Hope so that the model is, in a sense, optimizing its own update rule, not just its memory contents. So inference isn't just "apply a fixed learning rule to new data." The learning rule itself is something that's been learned and can keep adapting. That's the part I find most exciting, because it's the thing transformers structurally cannot do. A transformer can do in-context learning, but it can never improve at in-context learning while it's running.

So if I had to summarize, in the transformer paradigm inference is retrieval over a static system. In Hope, inference is continued learning in a system with multiple levels of memory, each adapting at its own timescale.

astra-6.text:
The main difference is that, in a standard transformer, inference and training are separate. During inference, the parameters are fixed. The model can use information in its context, but it isn’t updating its underlying memory through learning.

In Hope, we blur that boundary. The model has memory components that can continue updating as it processes information, and those components operate at different timescales. Some adapt quickly to what’s happening right now; others retain information over longer periods.

So inference becomes more than computing an answer with a fixed set of weights. It also involves updating the model’s internal memory. That doesn’t mean every parameter changes with every token—the important idea is that learning can happen within inference, at different rates.

sol-6.1.text:
The main difference is that inference is no longer just a forward pass through a fixed model. In a standard transformer, the parameters are frozen, and you adapt to the current conversation through the context window and the KV cache. You’re accumulating context, but you’re not updating the model’s learned memory.

In Hope, learning is part of inference. The model has memory components that can update as new information comes in, and those components operate at different timescales. Some adapt quickly to the immediate context; others change more slowly.

So the distinction between training and inference becomes less rigid. You still have a pretrained model, but during inference it can keep adapting its memory, rather than relying entirely on attending back to the tokens you’ve given it.
